I have been looking at trying to use the new variational calculus API on the harmonic oscillator (like we discussed here - I think it makes sense to give this potential its own topic). I have been trying to formalize the EquationOfMotion definition like the following:

noncomputable def EquationOfMotion (xₜ : Time → Space 1) : Prop :=
  ∀ t, (eulerLagrangeOp (lagrangian S) xₜ) t = 0

But this does not quite work due to

Application type mismatch: In the application
  eulerLagrangeOp S.lagrangian
the argument
  S.lagrangian
has type
  (Time → Space 1) → Time → ℝ : Type
but is expected to have type
  Time → Space 1 → Space 1 → ℝ : Type

Which makes sense. I have been able to write it like

noncomputable def lagrangian' : Time → Space 1 → Space 1 → ℝ :=
  fun (t : Time) (q : Space 1) (q_dot : Space 1) =>
    (1 / (2 : ℝ)) * S.m * ⟪q_dot, q_dot⟫_ℝ - (1 / (2 : ℝ)) * S.k * ⟪q, q⟫_ℝ

noncomputable def EquationOfMotion' (xₜ : Time → Space 1) : Prop :=
  ∀ t, (eulerLagrangeOp (lagrangian' S) xₜ) t = 0

Which I expect we can turn the former into somehow, I'm just not sure how. Does anyone have any ideas?

One approach might be to consider lagrangian' as the fundamental object, and derive lagrangian from that. I think it is true that there are various mathematical formulations of classical mechanics in which this is the correct direction (e.g. the jet bundle approach), but I can't speak for every formulation.

This might be a stupid question, but I was looking at the classical harmonic oscillator file and am confused by something: currently the Lagrangian is defined as follows: 

noncomputable def lagrangian (t : Time) (x : ConfigurationSpace)
    (v : ConfigurationSpace) : ℝ :=
  1 / (2 : ℝ) * S.m * ⟪v, v⟫_ℝ - S.potentialEnergy x

is it correct that x and v should both be of type ConfigurationSpace? My understanding is that ConfigurationSpace represents the space of positions, and the velocity belongs to something else (state space?) Any ideas on how we should clear this up or is my understanding incorrect? (I'm not really familiar with Lagrangian formulation, if the x and v are independent variables, where does the v = dx/dt relation come in?)

You are correct here. This is related to the difference between fderiv and mfderiv. Really ConfigurationSpace should have a manifold structure based on e.g. EuclideanSpace _ _, but instead it is inheriting its manifold structure from an inner-product structure. Similar changes to ConfigurationSpace need to be made as we made/are making to Space. This may actually be a nice thing to try doing, as there is not much which explicitly depends on ConfigurationSpace.

(The only reason you want the lagrangian as an explicit function of velocity is to write down the Euler-Lagrange equations more easily (and force etc). It is not strictly necessary and one can get away with just writing it as a function of the trajectory - which may be the better strategy here. )
hmm seems like ultimately we want something like lagrangian : TangentBundle _ ConfigurationSpace → ℝ?

I played around with this a bit more, I'm of the opinion that we should keep both the manifold version and the "undergraduate" version where we just treat velocity and position as EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1). I think the current issue is that ConfigurationSpace sits awkwardly somewhere in between the two representations, and if we have (xₜ : Time → ConfigurationSpace), then the type of ∂ₜ xₜ t is ConfigurationSpace which is incorrect. I guess this is what you mean by fderiv giving the wrong type but I don't see an easy fix here, maybe we should revert to the EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1) version for now?

(More generally, this could also be an illustrative example why the simple version is abusing definitions, and why the manifold version is "proper", and it would be nice if we can think about how physlib serves this pedagogical function.)

With the current formalization, one could make abbrev MomentumSpace := StrongDual ℝ ConfigurationSpace, although this is "abusing" the NormedAddCommGroup structure on ConfigurationSpace. Of course the proper thing would be the manifold structure.
it was about Lagrangian, not Hamiltonian... sorry for the noise

Just to give the physics behind what is going on here (I think), and to show that technically nothing is wrong with v : ConfigurationSpace - it just looks weird:

Physically ConfigurationSpace gets all the structure it has because there is an equivalence between ConfigurationSpace and Space and one can pull-back the structure on Space (not currently defined this way - although it should).

Note that Time has an implicit choice of units on it already, let's call it 'seconds'. So when we say the velocity is v : ConfigurationSpace we are really saying that in 1 second the configuration space will shift by a value v. In other-words that we have x + t * v.

So, actually, with the correct 'physics context', everything is fine here.

If one went to EuclideanSpace instead of ConfigurationSpace, the physics context would be exactly the same as I have written above.

I see two possible fixes:

  1. We include the physics context above and leave things as they are.
  2. We reduce the structure on ConfigurationSpace and Time which will force us to describe the velocity etc. in ways that will look less weird, although this will rely on a lot more complicated mathematics.

I think I here favor (1) as a temporary solution and (2) as a long-term solution.

I'd likely slightly push back on this: I think semantics matter in formalisation, and a name shouldn't be given to something which does not mean what it's supposed to.

In physics literature, as I understand it, ConfigurationSpace represents position and should not be used to represent velocities via this implicit identification. The current formalisation uses ConfigurationSpace for both, which I think is misleading. To me introducing the notionConfigurationSpace is to distinguish position from its tangent space (velocity), so if we're not modelling tangent spaces properly at the moment we should avoid it.

Allow me to restate your message this way: the "simpler" approach works because both configuration space and tangent space are isomorphic to EuclideanSpace in this coordinate setting, and we are effectively identifying everything with Euclidean Space and doing calculations there e.g. via fderiv.

I'd say working in the coordinate setting rather than the geometric setting is still a valid physics model, we just have to be clear about the context and what assumptions are made. Maybe we can have the geometric version as the "proper model", but a standalone file/folder for the coordinate model where we can have a less sophisticated model which physicists still use all the time. This will also allow us to point the less advanced user to an example toy model which imo is a good thing to be incorporated in physlib.

I agree that semantics matter is that v : ConfigurationSpace is bad :) - above I just wanted to understand why exactly it was present now. I think this coordinate point of view works for the classical harmonic oscillator, but it is not going to work for something like the pendulum, where the configuration space isn't isomorphic to EuclideanSpace. So maybe worth figuring out how to do this properly here. But I'm happy if we revert things back to EuclideanSpace in the mean time.

Maybe the best solution to this is:

  • Use Real (don't think we actually need EuclideanSpace here) in the Basic and Solution file instead of ConfigurationSpace
  • Add a comment to the Basic file about the fact we are working in coordinates.
  • Work on the API around ConfigurationSpace to make it easier to use so we can get the semantics right in a possible future refactor/addition of a proper model.
(we actually already have the coordinate system defined on ConfigurationSpace as valHomeomorphism)

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

-Use Real (don't think we actually need EuclideanSpace here)

If I remember correctly I think the idea was that using EuclideanSpace is more faithful to the quantities as vectors and compatible with generalisation to higher dimensions
Makes sense, let's do EuclideanSpace then. Will require a change to ConfigurationSpace to make its coordinate system based on EuclideanSpace too rather than Real, but this should be doable.

Hi all, I had a follow-up question from PR #1308.

@Joseph Tooby-Smith mentioned that maybe it was time to think about splitting HarmonicOscillator/Solution.lean into different parts.

I was planning on adding a TODO in the file for this, so we can mark it but I wanted some advice on how we should go about the split.

One possible split I had in mind was to keep Solution.lean as the umbrella import and move the main pieces into smaller files, maybe something like:

  • Solution/Basic.lean for trajectory construction and equation-of-motion facts
  • Solution/Energy.lean for energy-related lemmas
  • Solution/InitialData.lean for the alternative initial-condition parametrizations
  • Solution/AmplitudePhase.lean for amplitude-phase form
  • Solution/SpecialTimes.lean for velocity-zero times, turning points, and zero crossings
  • Solution/Periodicity.lean for period/recurrence facts

But I was wondering whether this is too large of a split to be useful at the moment. Another lighter option would maybe be a two file split where we move out the amplitude-phase, special properties of the trajectory and periodicity.

What do you guys think would be most productive at the moment.

I think there is no harm in the large split. This will make smaller files, which are more focused. I don't see anything wrong with that, and the titles you have chosen make it obvious what is in each file so things will still be easy to find.

Perfect, I'll proceed in this direction.

Thank you.
